## Design direction agreed in Slack gang grill (2026-07-10)

Source: https://slack.com/archives/C0BE69AHCQP/p1783709543707769

The group agreed to proceed without prematurely optimizing storage:

- Tools are canonical capabilities; ordinary tool authors need not know CodeMode exists.
- Visible tools default into CodeMode. Exceptional provider-level tools opt out with `codemode: false`; `execute` itself opts out to avoid recursion.
- Public Promise and Effect tool drafts should support flat definitions through `draft.add({ ... })`, without requiring `Tool.make(...)` in normal usage.
- `namespace?: string`, `codemode?: boolean`, and `pinned?: boolean` are first-class Tool-definition fields.
- Namespace paths use validated dotted strings for nesting, e.g. `slack.admin.users`; do not silently sanitize segments.
- Optional namespace metadata is additive (`draft.namespace.add(...)`). A namespaced tool implicitly creates its namespace when no metadata was registered.
- MCP server names naturally become namespaces. MCP server `instructions` remain their existing Instruction source rather than being treated as concise namespace summaries.
- `pinned` applies only to CodeMode tools; `{ codemode: false, pinned: true }` is invalid.
- Small catalogs inline every full signature. Larger catalogs use namespace summaries plus pinned signatures, selected by a configurable token budget (initially 2,000), not raw tool count.
- Changing tools, permissions, or selected agent produces semantic added/removed/signature-changed Instruction updates; use a full replacement when smaller or when rendering mode changes. Denied tools are omitted entirely.
- CodeMode owns canonical descriptors, namespace/pinned semantics, search indexing, compact/full planning, structural diffing, and pure initial/change rendering. OpenCode owns agent/permission filtering, budget configuration, and durable Instruction chronology.
- Store one deterministic, model-facing catalog snapshot as a content-addressed Instruction value. It contains descriptors only—not executors or raw API specs. Revisit per-tool blobs only if measured catalog churn makes whole-snapshot storage costly.

Still open for implementation-level iteration:

- exact namespace metadata field (`summary` vs `description`) and compact rendering syntax
- exact simplified catalog-search runtime surface
- strict framing of MCP-authored descriptions when rendered through privileged Instructions

Related architecture tracker: #35364.

I would like to take this one. The diagnosis in the report looks right: the request fiber is only interrupted on ServerResponse close, which Bun does not emit for dropped SSE clients, so the event stream keeps writing into a dead socket. My plan is to wire disconnect detection to IncomingMessage close and aborted in the event stream path so the stream terminates regardless of response close propagation, add a regression test, and try to pin down a deterministic repro for the CPU spin.

Hi! I’ve built a lightweight solution that addresses exactly this feature request. 

It’s called **opencode-remote**: a wrapper and WebSocket bridge that mirrors your running local terminal session (1:1 mirror using Node.js IPC, not a separate process) to a mobile-optimized Progressive Web App (PWA) using `xterm.js`. 

This setup allows you to:
- Monitor terminal output in real-time on your mobile device.
- Send new tasks and accept/deny agent permissions remotely when away from your desk.
- Keep the exact terminal state synchronized thanks to dynamic terminal resizing and alternate screen buffer restoration.
- Set up a secure Cloudflare Tunnel automatically with a single command (no port forwarding required).

You can find the repository, instructions, and architecture diagrams here: https://github.com/cmateos91/opencode-remote

Hope this is helpful or inspires future native remote control designs!

## Final gang-grill corrections

The detailed handoff supersedes the earlier comment where they differ: https://slack.com/archives/C0BE69AHCQP/p1783726066302709

Key corrections from the remainder of the grill:

- A path may be both callable and a namespace (`tools.slack.admin(...)` and `tools.slack.admin.invite(...)`). The earlier recommendation to reject leaf/branch conflicts was reversed.
- Leave the current `await tools.$codemode.search({ query, namespace, limit, offset })` API and paginated result unchanged for now. Synchronous/string search ideas were deferred.
- Keep JavaScript `await` and `Promise.all`; do not add Haxl-style query/command machinery.
- Recompute the visible catalog only during ordinary LLM request assembly; add no Tool watchers, Session wakeups, or timers.
- If no CodeMode Tools are visible, omit `execute`, CodeMode Instructions, and empty namespaces.
- The remaining questions about namespaced native flattening, compact fallback prose, and public budget configuration were explicitly deferred for implementation.

The cold-location investigation produced two merged improvements:

- #36290 removed eager Snapshot repository setup from Location acquisition. Bracketed medians improved from roughly 463 ms to 134 ms for one cold location and 1,954 ms to 707 ms for the slowest concurrent location.
- #36321 reduced subsequent Git discovery from three subprocesses to one. The final alternating benchmark improved the five-repository batch from 33.2 ms to 11.5 ms.

Config existence checks and Location build concurrency caps were measured and discarded. Keeping this issue open because coordinated update/replacement UX, SSE readiness under load, and the reported CPU/memory behavior remain unresolved.

Implementation note: the V2 TUI currently receives each model’s `providerID` and the available provider list, but subscription models do not expose their backing provider as structured metadata. For example, the TUI can tell that GPT-5.6 Sol comes through `opencode`, but not that its backing provider is OpenAI.

This means we can shorten the prompt label to `Anomaly` and detect whether any BYOK provider is configured, but we cannot reliably render `Anomaly (OpenAI)` only when OpenAI overlaps. Inferring this from model names or IDs would be brittle. ## Durable supervisor option

A separate process supervisor is worth keeping as an explicit design alternative rather than assuming every shell must be cancelled at server teardown.

The narrow first scope would be **survive managed server restarts, not supervisor or machine restarts**:

```text
managed server <-> authenticated local RPC <-> job supervisor -> command process tree
                                                |
                                                +-> durable job rows + output files
                                                +-> durable Session inbox completion
```

The supervisor remains the process owner while the HTTP/session server restarts, so the new server never adopts a bare PID. A durable job record would at least carry job ID, owner Session/tool call, command metadata, status, timeout, process identity owned by the supervisor, output path/cursor, and terminal outcome. Completion or interruption must be admitted to the owning Session inbox before the supervisor considers delivery complete.

Useful first-scope semantics:

- Normal server upgrade/restart leaves the supervisor and its children running.
- The replacement server reconnects, lists jobs, and resumes observation through versioned local RPC.
- A supervisor or machine restart does **not** replay commands. On the next boot, unfinished jobs become durably `interrupted` unless a later design adds stronger per-job ownership.
- Cancellation remains process-tree-aware and explicit on POSIX and Windows.
- Server/supervisor version skew and service election are part of the deployment contract.

This is medium-sized if the supervisor is guaranteed to outlive only server restarts. It becomes substantially larger if the supervisor itself must be restartable: that needs per-job wrappers or another OS ownership mechanism, fencing, PID-reuse protection, upgrade handoff, and orphan reconciliation.

The safe cancellation-first design should remain the baseline. The supervisor is the option to choose if product semantics require background commands to keep running through routine server upgrades.

## Follow-up: permission preflight and persisted forms

The permission path can be made significantly more restartable if authorization is an explicit phase **before any physical tool side effect**.

A useful durable distinction is:

```text
tool call: authorizing -> executing -> settled
permission request: pending -> approved | rejected
```

Recovery may reconstruct an `authorizing` call, but must never replay an ambiguous `executing` call. Permission request IDs should be deterministic for the owning tool call (and request ordinal/resource set), with the request payload and terminal answer persisted. After all required approvals are present, transition the tool call to `executing` durably before entering the body.

Most current built-ins already place `permission.assert(...)` before their physical side effects, but this is a convention inside each executor rather than an enforceable phase. Several tools perform path resolution/inspection first and some issue multiple permission assertions. A restartable design therefore needs one of:

- an explicit tool authorization/preparation seam that computes every request before execution; or
- a built-in-only resumable protocol with a tested invariant that all work before the final authorization barrier is safe to repeat.

Dynamic/plugin tools and MCP calls should remain non-replayable unless they opt into that contract. In particular, an MCP elicitation may occur after a remote call has already started, so the generic permission/form recovery rule cannot safely replay it.

Persisting form CRUD state itself is straightforward: durable form row, payload, owner Session, status, answer, and compare-and-set reply/cancel. `Form.ask` should use a deterministic owner ID and rejoin an existing pending or answered form after reconstruction. Shutdown must not publish a user cancellation merely because the Location graph is closing.

The continuation still matters:

- The built-in question tool is a good first target because it has no physical work between authorization and `Form.ask`; it can safely reconstruct and rejoin the durable form.
- API-created/global forms can persist independently without resuming a tool.
- Forms raised mid-side-effect (notably MCP elicitation) need a separate resumable protocol or an explicit interrupted outcome.

Focused recovery coverage should prove: restart while authorizing, approval/rejection before and after the new process attaches, answer/cancel before and after reconstruction, no replay once `executing`, deterministic retry IDs, and changed path/resource resolution causing a fresh authorization rather than using an approval for a different target.
